```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _lib.orplot import new_axes, shade_polygon, clip_halfplane, mark_point, COLORS
from _lib.toy_lp import A, b, c, vertices, solve

V = vertices()
LO, HI = -0.5, 8.5

def clip_box(poly, lo=LO, hi=HI):
    for a, beta in [((1, 0), hi), ((-1, 0), -lo), ((0, 1), hi), ((0, -1), -lo)]:
        poly = clip_halfplane(poly, a, beta)
    return poly

def level_segment(cvec, z, lo=LO, hi=HI):
    """Endpoints of the line c.x = z inside the plotting box."""
    big = [(lo, lo), (hi, lo), (hi, hi), (lo, hi)]
    strip = clip_halfplane(clip_halfplane(big, cvec, z + 1e-6), -np.asarray(cvec), -z + 1e-6)
    if len(strip) < 2:
        return None
    P = np.array(strip)
    d = np.array([-cvec[1], cvec[0]])
    proj = P @ d
    return [P[np.argmin(proj)].tolist(), P[np.argmax(proj)].tolist()]

def optimal_face(cvec, V=V, tol=1e-9):
    vals = V @ cvec
    best = vals.max()
    return V[vals >= best - tol], float(best)
```

## The idea

With two variables, an LP can be solved by drawing it. Shade the **feasible region**
(all points satisfying every constraint). Then draw lines of equal objective value,
$c^\top x = z$; they are parallel, and moving them in the direction of $c$ increases $z$.
Slide the line as far as it goes while still touching the region. The last point (or
points) it touches is optimal.

```{python}
#| label: fig-graphical
#| fig-cap: "The workshop LP. The feasible region (grey) is bounded by the wood and labor constraints and the axes. Lines of equal profit $3x_1 + 4x_2 = z$ (dashed) move toward the upper right as $z$ grows. The last feasible point they touch is the vertex $(2, 3)$, with profit $18$."
sol = solve()
fig, ax = new_axes(1, xlim=(LO, HI), ylim=(LO, HI), size=4.6)
shade_polygon(ax, V, "#888888", alpha=0.18, lw=1.8)
for z in (6, 12, 18, 24):
    seg = level_segment(c, z)
    if seg:
        style = dict(color=COLORS["hull"], lw=1.2 if z != 18 else 2.0,
                     ls="--" if z != 18 else "-", alpha=0.85)
        ax.plot(*np.array(seg).T, **style)
        left = min(seg, key=lambda q: q[0])
        ax.text(left[0] + 0.12, left[1] + 0.12, f"$z={z}$", fontsize=9,
                color=COLORS["hull"])
ax.annotate("", xy=(4.6, 6.2), xytext=(3.4, 4.6),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["hull"], lw=1.6))
ax.text(4.65, 6.25, "$c=(3,4)$", color=COLORS["hull"], fontsize=10)
mark_point(ax, sol["x"], COLORS["weak"])
ax.annotate(r"$x^\star = (2,3)$", sol["x"], xytext=(-62, -18), textcoords="offset points")
ax.text(5.0, 1.2, "wood:\n$x_1 + 2x_2 \\leq 8$", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["p1"])
ax.text(0.45, 7.75, "labor: $2x_1 + x_2 \\leq 7$", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["p2"])
ax.plot([LO, HI], [(8 - LO) / 2, (8 - HI) / 2], color=COLORS["p1"], lw=1, alpha=0.6)
ax.plot([(7 - HI) / 2, (7 - LO) / 2], [HI, LO], color=COLORS["p2"], lw=1, alpha=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Notice where the optimum is: at a **corner** of the region, where two constraints are
tight. Both wood and labor are used up completely. This is no accident.

## Explore: turn the objective

```{python}
#| label: geom-ojs-data
#| echo: false
geom = []
for deg in range(360):
    th = np.deg2rad(deg)
    cv = np.array([np.cos(th), np.sin(th)])
    F, z = optimal_face(cv)
    geom.append(dict(deg=deg, c=cv.round(4).tolist(), face=F.round(4).tolist(),
                     z=round(z, 3), level=level_segment(cv, z)))
ojs_define(geom=geom, geomRegion=V.round(4).tolist(), geomColors=COLORS,
           geomBox=[LO, HI])
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Interactive.** Turn the objective direction $c$. The optimal vertex stays put for a
while and then jumps to the next one. At the two directions where $c$ is perpendicular
to an edge (straight left and straight down), the whole edge is optimal.
:::


```{ojs}
    svg.append("line").attr("y1", y(t)).attr("y2", y(t)).attr("x1", x(lo)).attr("x2", x(hi))
       .attr("stroke", C.grid).attr("stroke-opacity", t === 0 ? 0.9 : 0.35);
  }
  svg.append("path").attr("d", path(geomRegion)).attr("fill", "#888888")
     .attr("fill-opacity", 0.2).attr("stroke", "#888888").attr("stroke-width", 1.6);
  if (R.level) svg.append("line").attr("x1", x(R.level[0][0])).attr("y1", y(R.level[0][1]))
     .attr("x2", x(R.level[1][0])).attr("y2", y(R.level[1][1]))
     .attr("stroke", C.hull).attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("stroke-dasharray", "7 4");
  if (R.face.length > 1) {
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", x(R.face[0][0])).attr("y1", y(R.face[0][1]))
       .attr("x2", x(R.face[1][0])).attr("y2", y(R.face[1][1]))
       .attr("stroke", C.weak).attr("stroke-width", 7).attr("stroke-linecap", "round");
  }
  for (const v of geomRegion)
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x(v[0])).attr("cy", y(v[1])).attr("r", 4)
       .attr("fill", "currentColor");
  for (const v of R.face)
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x(v[0])).attr("cy", y(v[1])).attr("r", 8)
       .attr("fill", C.weak).attr("stroke", "white").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
  // objective arrow, drawn in the empty upper-right corner
  const o = [6.4, 6.4];
  const tip = [o[0] + 1.5 * R.c[0], o[1] + 1.5 * R.c[1]];
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x(o[0])).attr("cy", y(o[1])).attr("r", 3).attr("fill", C.hull);
  svg.append("defs").append("marker").attr("id", "geom-arrow").attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
     .attr("refX", 9).attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 7).attr("markerHeight", 7)
     .attr("orient", "auto-start-reverse").append("path").attr("d", "M0,0L10,5L0,10Z")
     .attr("fill", C.hull);
  svg.append("line").attr("x1", x(o[0])).attr("y1", y(o[1])).attr("x2", x(tip[0]))
     .attr("y2", y(tip[1])).attr("stroke", C.hull).attr("stroke-width", 2.4)
     .attr("marker-end", "url(#geom-arrow)");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", x(tip[0]) + 6).attr("y", y(tip[1]) - 4)
     .attr("fill", C.hull).text("c");
  return svg.node();
}
```

```{python}
fig, axes = new_axes(3, xlim=(LO, HI), ylim=(LO, HI), size=3.2)
for ax, deg in zip(axes, (20, 53, 180)):

    F, z = optimal_face(cv)
    shade_polygon(ax, V, "#888888", alpha=0.18, lw=1.4)
    seg = level_segment(cv, z)
    if seg:
        ax.plot(*np.array(seg).T, color=COLORS["hull"], ls="--", lw=1.4)
    if len(F) > 1:
        ax.plot(*F.T, color=COLORS["weak"], lw=6, solid_capstyle="round")

        mark_point(ax, v, COLORS["weak"])
    o = np.array([6.4, 6.4])
    ax.annotate("", xy=o + 1.6 * cv, xytext=o,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["hull"], lw=1.6))
    ax.set_title(f"direction {deg}°", fontsize=11)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## The math

### Four possible outcomes

Every LP falls into exactly one of these cases.

```{python}
#| label: fig-outcomes
#| fig-cap: "The four outcomes of an LP. (1) A unique optimal vertex. (2) Several optima: the objective is parallel to an edge, and the whole edge (red) is optimal. (3) Unbounded: the region extends forever in a direction that improves the objective (arrow), so there is no optimum. (4) Infeasible: the constraints contradict each other and no point satisfies all of them."
fig, axes = new_axes(4, xlim=(LO, HI), ylim=(LO, HI), size=2.9)
# 1 unique
ax = axes[0]
shade_polygon(ax, V, "#888888", alpha=0.18, lw=1.4)
mark_point(ax, (2, 3), COLORS["weak"])
ax.set_title("(1) unique optimum", fontsize=10)
# 2 multiple: c = (1, 2) is parallel to the wood edge
ax = axes[1]
shade_polygon(ax, V, "#888888", alpha=0.18, lw=1.4)
F, z = optimal_face(np.array([1.0, 2.0]))
ax.plot(*F.T, color=COLORS["weak"], lw=6, solid_capstyle="round")
ax.set_title("(2) a whole edge optimal", fontsize=10)
# 3 unbounded
ax = axes[2]
U = clip_box(clip_halfplane(clip_halfplane(
    [(0, 0), (60, 0), (60, 60), (0, 60)], (-1, 1), 2), (1, -2), 2))
shade_polygon(ax, U, "#888888", alpha=0.18, lw=1.4)
ax.annotate("", xy=(7.6, 6.8), xytext=(4.8, 4.4),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["hull"], lw=2))
ax.text(1.2, 7.6, r"max $x_1 + x_2$", fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("(3) unbounded", fontsize=10)
# 4 infeasible
ax = axes[3]
quad = [(0, 0), (60, 0), (60, 60), (0, 60)]
shade_polygon(ax, clip_box(clip_halfplane(quad, (1, 1), 2)), COLORS["p1"], alpha=0.3, lw=1.4)
shade_polygon(ax, clip_box(clip_halfplane(quad, (-1, -1), -5)), COLORS["p2"], alpha=0.3, lw=1.4)
ax.text(0.3, 0.7, r"$x_1+x_2 \leq 2$", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["p1"])
ax.text(3.4, 6.6, r"$x_1+x_2 \geq 5$", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["p2"])
ax.set_title("(4) infeasible", fontsize=10)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel(""); ax.set_ylabel("")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (fundamental theorem of linear programming)
For an LP $\max\{c^\top x : Ax \le b\}$, exactly one of the following holds:

1. it is **infeasible**: no $x$ satisfies $Ax \le b$;
2. it is **unbounded**: there are feasible points with arbitrarily large $c^\top x$;
3. it has an **optimal solution**.

In case 3, if the feasible region has at least one vertex (for example, whenever
$x \ge 0$ is among the constraints), then some vertex is optimal. The set of all optimal
solutions is a face of the feasible region: a vertex, an edge, or a larger face.
:::

The theorem has three consequences that the rest of LP theory builds on.

- **No "almost optimal" trap.** A bounded, feasible LP always attains its optimum. (A
  nonlinear problem such as $\min\ 1/x$ over $x \ge 1$ need not.)
- **Finitely many candidates.** It is enough to search the vertices, of which there are
  finitely many. The simplex method does exactly that, cleverly.
- **Every outcome has a certificate.** An optimal $x$ comes with dual prices proving it
  optimal ([LP Duality](../duality/lp-duality.qmd)); infeasibility comes with a Farkas
  vector ([Farkas' Lemma](../../foundations/polyhedra/farkas-lemma.qmd)); unboundedness
  comes with a ray $r$ of the region with $c^\top r > 0$.

## Why it works

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch
If the LP is feasible and $c^\top x$ is bounded above on the feasible region $P$, write
$P = \operatorname{conv}(V) + \operatorname{cone}(R)$ by the
[Minkowski–Weyl theorem](../../foundations/polyhedra/minkowski-weyl.qmd). Boundedness
forces $c^\top r \le 0$ for every ray $r \in R$ (otherwise moving along $r$ would increase
the objective forever). So for any $x = \sum_i \lambda_i v^i + \sum_j \mu_j r^j$ in $P$,
$$
c^\top x \le \sum_i \lambda_i\, c^\top v^i \le \max_i c^\top v^i ,
$$
and the best of the finitely many points $v^i$ is optimal. When $P$ has vertices, the
$v^i$ can be taken to be the vertices. The full argument is on
[Polyhedra and Their Vertices](../../foundations/polyhedra/polyhedra-and-vertices.qmd).
:::

## In practice

- **Real LPs have thousands of dimensions**, so nobody draws them, but the picture
  stays the same: a polyhedron, a direction, a best corner.
- **Ties are common.** Real models often have many optimal solutions (case 2). Solvers
  return one of them, and a tiny change of data can switch which one.
- **Unbounded usually means a modeling error**, such as a missing constraint. Infeasible
  usually means a data or modeling error, and the Farkas vector shows which constraints
  conflict.
